4&(2,2)\\
5&(1,4),(4,1)\\
6&(0,6),(3,3),(6,0)\\
7&(2,5),(5,2)
\end{array}
\]

A product is nonzero exactly when all three indices of a line are nonzero.

### Case \(m=0\)

All \(x_i=0\), so both conditions hold. This gives
\[
1
\]
tuple.

### Case \(m=2\)

Every product contains a zero, so \(P=0\). Choose the two nonzero positions and assign them \(1,-1\):
\[
\binom72\cdot2=42.
\]

### Case \(m=3\)

The three nonzero signs must all be equal. If the three positions form a line, the corresponding product is \(\pm1\), so \(P\not\equiv0\pmod3\). Otherwise every product contains a zero.

Of the \(\binom73=35\) three-element sets, \(7\) are lines. Hence
\[
(35-7)\cdot2=56.
\]

### Case \(m=4\)

The signs must be two \(1\)'s and two \(-1\)'s. A four-element set can contain at most one line, since two distinct lines have union of size \(5\). The number containing a line is
\[
7\binom41=28.
\]
These fail because \(P\) is a single nonzero product. The remaining \(35-28=7\) sets give \(P=0\). Thus
\[
7\binom42=42.
\]

### Case \(m=5\)

Choose the two zero positions. Each lies on \(3\) lines, and they share one line, so \(3+3-1=5\) lines meet the zero set. Therefore exactly two lines are contained in the five nonzero positions. These two lines intersect in one position and together cover all five positions.

The sum condition requires either one \(1\) and four \(-1\)'s, or one \(-1\) and four \(1\)'s.

- If the unique minority sign is at the intersection of the two lines, both line products are equal, so their sum is \(\pm2\not\equiv0\).
- If it is at one of the other four positions, exactly one line product is changed, so the two products are opposite and cancel.

Thus there are \(4+4=8\) valid sign assignments for each zero pair:
\[
\binom72\cdot8=21\cdot8=168.
\]

### Case \(m=6\)

Fix the zero position. Exactly four lines avoid it. These four lines can be viewed as the vertices of \(K_4\): each of the six nonzero positions is the intersection of a unique pair of these lines, hence corresponds to an edge of \(K_4\).

If all six signs are equal, then \(P\equiv\pm4\not\equiv0\pmod3\). Therefore the sum condition forces three \(1\)'s and three \(-1\)'s.

Choose the three edges corresponding to negative signs. A line product is negative exactly when an odd number of its three incident edges are negative. Since \(P\) is then a sum of four numbers \(\pm1\), it is divisible by \(3\) exactly when two line products are positive and two are negative.

Thus the selected three edges must give exactly two odd-degree vertices in \(K_4\). This happens exactly when they form a path of length \(3\) through all four vertices. The number of such paths is
\[
\frac{4!}{2}=12.
\]
There are \(7\) choices for the zero position, giving
\[
7\cdot12=84.
\]

### Case \(m=7\)

The sign distribution is either two \(1\)'s and five \(-1\)'s, or five \(1\)'s and two \(-1\)'s.

Start with all signs equal and flip the two minority signs. Each index lies on three lines, and the two indices share one line. Hence
\[
3+3-2=4
\]
line products are flipped.

- With two \(1\)'s and five \(-1\)'s, this leaves three negative and four positive line products, so \(P\equiv4-3=1\pmod3\).
- With five \(1\)'s and two \(-1\)'s, this leaves four negative and three positive line products, so \(P\equiv3-4\equiv2\pmod3\).

Thus there are no valid tuples with \(m=7\).

Adding all cases,
\[
1+42+56+42+168+84=393.
\]

\[
\boxed{393}
\]
